newsitem.title: USA: Murder charges against arson suspect thrown out.
newsitem.headline: Murder charges against arson suspect thrown out.

text.p: Washington state's highest court Thursday threw out murder charges against the suspect in a warehouse fire that killed four firefighters.

In a 5-4 decision, the state Supreme Court ruled that prosecutors must follow a 1995 ruling by Brazil's Supreme Court, which allowed suspect Martin Pang to be extradited on condition he be charged only with first-degree arson.
The court said that under the extradition treaty between the two countries, "Brazil, as the requested state, has sole authority to determine whether a particular offence is extraditable."
King County Prosecutor Norm Maleng said he would appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Pang, 41, was the chief suspect from the outset in the January 1995 fire that destroyed his parents' frozen food warehouse in Seattle's International District.

According to court documents, he had talked for years about burning down the warehouse to collect insurance proceeds, and he allegedly told a friend afterward that "nobody was supposed to get hurt, the building was just supposed to burn down."

Pang fled the country and was arrested in Rio de Janeiro in March 1995. He was extradited nearly a year later after Brazil resisted pressure to reverse its Supreme Court decision despite requests from President Clinton, then-Secretary of State Warren Christopher and other U.S. leaders.
Although arson is punishable by a maximum life sentence in Washington state, convicted first-time offenders are generally sentenced to no more than 27 months in prison.
Prosecutors have said they would press for a longer sentence in this case, although the Supreme Court said judges usually are bound by sentencing guidelines.
If convicted on four counts of first-degree murder, Pang would have faced a minimum 80-year sentence.
Pang's attorney John Henry Browne said Pangs' parents' were "very relieved" by the ruling.

In a dissenting opinion, state Supreme Court Chief Justice Barbara Durham sided with a lower court in saying the murder prosecution should be allowed because it would be based on the same set of facts presented to Brazil's high court.

"Under the majority's holding, the deaths of four innocent victims will go unpunished, even though the laws of both Brazil and Washington recognise arson resulting in death as a more serious crime than arson alone," she wrote.
Pang remains in King County jail, where he has been held on $5 million bail since his extradition.
